summary: Specified a DKIM adjunct called Author Domain Signing Practices, letting a domain publish how it signs mail so receivers could judge messages lacking a valid signature from the author's domain. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: ADSP let an email domain publish whether it signed its outgoing messages with DKIM. This memo defines the record and lookup procedure, and discusses the risks of relying on the result.

questions: where is the adsp record published
subtitle: A DNS-published statement of how an email domain signs messages, now a Historic mechanism.

tldr.problem: A missing DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) signature does not by itself show that a message is forged, but some domains wanted to state that they signed all outgoing mail.
tldr.mechanism: Author Domain Signing Practices (ADSP) lets a domain publish a DNS TXT record with its signing practice, which a receiver can check against the domain in the message's From address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5617 is Historic and was updated by RFC 8553. Its ADSP mechanism should be understood as historical rather than a current recommendation.

today: RFC 5617 is Historic and was updated by RFC 8553. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: What ADSP Was Intended to Do
sections.content:
DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) lets a signing domain attach a cryptographic signature to a message. A receiver can verify the signature using a public key retrieved from the signer's domain. But many messages may have no signature, and absence of a signature does not by itself indicate forgery.

Author Domain Signing Practices (ADSP) lets a domain publish statements about whether it signs mail that uses that domain in the From field. An Author Domain Signature is a valid DKIM signature whose d= domain matches the domain in an Author Address. This document defines how a host checks for a domain's practice.
sections.plainLanguage: A DKIM signature can show that a domain signed a message, but an unsigned message is not automatically forged. ADSP gave a domain a way to publish whether it expected to sign its mail.

sections.title: How Receivers Use an ADSP Result
sections.content:
A receiver looks up the practice for each Author Domain in the message's From address. The lookup is most relevant when a message lacks a valid Author Domain Signature. If such a signature is present, the ADSP result adds no benefit for that domain; a valid signature from another domain may still be considered alongside the result.

The result can say that the domain might or might not sign mail, that all mail is signed, or that all mail is signed and unsigned mail should be discarded. A fourth result says the domain is outside ADSP's scope because it does not exist in DNS. A temporary DNS failure can leave the lookup without a result. ADSP has no effect unless another system acts on the result.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver checks the domain's published practice, especially when the message lacks a matching signature. The record provides guidance; another mail system must decide what to do with it.

sections.title: The DNS Record and Lookup Procedure
sections.content:
ADSP records are DNS TXT records at a name formed by adding _adsp._domainkey. before the Author Domain. A record begins with the dkim= tag, whose defined values are unknown, all, and discardable. An unrecognized value is treated as unknown. ADSP applies to one domain, not its parent or child domains, and records must not use wildcard names.

A checker first determines whether the Author Domain exists in DNS; NXDOMAIN means it is out of scope, while NODATA is different. It then queries the domain's ADSP TXT record. A single valid record is used. No record produces the default unknown result. Multiple records or an invalid record make the result undefined. A DNS SERVFAIL ends the lookup without a result.
sections.plainLanguage: The domain publishes one TXT record under a special DNS name. A receiver first checks that the domain exists, then reads that record; missing or failed DNS results have different meanings.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Cautions
sections.content:
The threat considered is a sender claiming to be an Author who did not authorize the message. The memo says there is no empirical evidence about how much this type of domain-name misuse contributes to recipient deception or whether stopping it would have a significant effect. Checkers may also create traffic-multiplication risks by looking up domains named in fraudulent messages.

DNS wildcards can interfere with determining whether an Author Domain exists, so domains publishing practices other than unknown should not use wildcards. Message forwarding, mailing lists, or other processing can modify a message and invalidate a DKIM signature. The appendix cautions that publishing discardable can cause some legitimate mail to be discarded. The RFC also registers the ADSP tags, practices, and authentication-result names with IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: ADSP could not prove that an unsigned message was forged, and ordinary mail processing could invalidate a signature. A domain that asked receivers to discard unsigned mail risked losing legitimate messages too.

viz.caption: VALUES OF THE dkim= ADSP TAG

items.label: Unknown
items.desc: The domain might sign some or all email.

items.label: All
items.desc: All domain mail is signed with an Author Domain Signature.

items.label: Discardable
items.desc: All mail is signed; recipients are encouraged to discard mail without a valid matching signature.
